notes.meaning: The bridegroom admires his bride starting from her feet and moving upward, praising her graceful movements. Her jeweled sandals show that she is free and treated with royal dignity, not a barefoot servant. In traditional spiritual readings, this describes the church walking in the peace of the gospel and clothed with the honor Christ gives her.

Her body is compared to the richness and plenty of a royal banquet. The pictures of wine in a well-shaped bowl and a mound of wheat framed by lilies speak of health, beauty, and fullness of life. Christian teachers historically saw this as the abundant spiritual food and blessing the church provides for her children.

Her breasts are compared to two young gazelles that match each other in beauty and balance. This gentle picture highlights innocence, charm, and the natural beauty of married love. Older commentators often saw these twins as pictures of faith and love working together in the believer's life.

Her neck is compared to a white ivory tower, showing both upright dignity and pure beauty. Her eyes are quiet and sparkling like the clear pools of the city of Heshbon, while her profile is noble and striking like a watchtower in Lebanon. Believers have long seen in these images the quiet peace and clear spiritual sight of the church.

Her head is held high and fruitful like the famous slopes of Mount Carmel, and her glossy dark hair shines with royal purple tones. The king is so captivated by her beauty that he is held fast by love and cannot look away. Traditionally, this shows how deeply Christ delights in His people and loves to dwell in sweet fellowship with them.

The speaker pauses his detailed list to express pure wonder at how charming and lovely his bride is. She brings him deep delight in every way. In spiritual reflection, this shows Christ rejoicing over His church, whom He has made lovely through His own grace.

Her tall and upright posture is compared to a graceful palm tree that stays green through every season. Her beauty offers sweet nourishment, like rich clusters of fruit hanging from the tree. In the life of faith, this represents a believer who stays upright under trial and bears good fruit for God.

The husband expresses his joyful desire to hold his bride close and enjoy the fullness of married love. He longs for her sweet embrace, comparing her kisses to grapes and her breath to fresh apples. Older writers saw this as the Lord drawing near to enjoy the devotion and righteous fruit of His people.

Her loving words and kisses are compared to the finest wine that flows smoothly and brings sweet refreshment. In this loving dialogue, their affection restores and gladdens their hearts. Commentators saw this as a picture of the church speaking gracious words of truth and praise that bring delight to Christ.

The bride speaks with full confidence, resting in the truth that she belongs completely to her beloved and that he deeply desires her. Her words show a secure and selfless love that rejoices in his affection. For Christians, this is a beloved picture of the believer's absolute assurance of being united to Christ, who loved His people from the beginning.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars understand the Song as a story of three characters, where the young woman here rejects King Solomon and declares her faithful love to a rural shepherd.

notes.meaning: Having received her husband's praise, the bride invites him to leave the busy city and travel out to the quiet countryside. She wants uninterrupted time where they can walk together and rest in nature. Spiritually, this shows the soul's desire to withdraw from worldly noise and spend quiet time in prayer and communion with Christ.

She suggests getting up early to visit the vineyards and watch the spring blossoms appear on the vines and pomegranates. In that private, blossoming setting, she promises to give him all her affection. Traditionally, this points to believers actively watching for spiritual life in the church and pouring out their best love for their Lord.

The fragrance of mandrakes, widely known in the ancient world as plants of love, shows that the season of romance has arrived. The bride has saved all kinds of delicious gifts, both tried and new, exclusively for the man she loves. In the Christian life, this pictures believers offering all their varied gifts, duties, and devotion to Christ alone.
